analysis.one_liner: Requires certified training for subprime mortgage lenders and brokers and bans forced arbitration in consumer contracts.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors, the bill never advanced past its referral to the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required anyone lending to or brokering for subprime mortgage borrowers to pass a HUD-administered exam on lending law and predatory practices, with certification revocable for violations. It would have barred lenders from charging fees never disclosed up front, required a plain-language rights summary 24 hours before closing, banned pressuring appraisers to inflate home values, and imposed fines up to $10,000 per day for unfair or deceptive practices. It also would have made mandatory arbitration clauses unenforceable in consumer contracts, so consumers could take disputes to court.
analysis.who_benefits: Home buyers and homeowners in the subprime market, who would gain better-trained loan originators, upfront fee disclosures, protection from appraisal pressure, and court access instead of forced arbitration. The protections would extend to all consumers signing standard contracts, since the arbitration ban covered any consumer transaction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Subprime borrowers and consumers with contracts

how_it_helps.text: Anyone providing subprime mortgage lending or brokerage services would have to be certified by HUD as trained in federal lending law and in what constitutes predatory lending, with certification revocable for unfair or deceptive practices.

Lenders making high-cost mortgages would have to maintain a federally regulated best-practices compliance plan, train and evaluate their employees and agents, and resolve consumer complaints within 60 days without any collection action during that window.

Lenders could not impose any charge or fee on a high-cost mortgage that was not disclosed before the loan was signed, and consumers would receive a plain-language summary of their rights at least 24 hours before closing.

The bill would have made it unlawful to compensate, coerce, or intimidate an appraiser to inflate a home's value, and to submit a knowingly false appraisal, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day for a first violation and $20,000 per day for repeat violations.

Mandatory binding arbitration clauses in consumer contracts would become unenforceable, letting consumers sue in court; businesses could still use arbitration if the consumer agreed to it after a dispute actually arose.
The bill would have authorized $2 million per year in grants to nonprofit community development corporations to educate borrowers and community groups about predatory lending.

analysis.who_pays: Subprime mortgage lenders and brokers, who would bear the cost of training, testing, and certification, exposure to daily civil penalties, and limits on undisclosed fees. Banks and other businesses that relied on mandatory arbitration clauses to keep consumer disputes out of court would lose that shield across all consumer transactions, not just mortgages.

drawbacks.text: A certification and examination regime for every subprime loan originator would add compliance costs to a lending segment that serves the riskiest borrowers, and those costs or tighter underwriting could translate into fewer or more expensive loans for exactly the people the bill was meant to protect.

The bill's central terms — including the legal definition of 'predatory lending' and which loan characteristics count as 'subprime' — would have been left to later regulation by HUD and the Federal Reserve, so its practical effect depended heavily on how agencies wrote the rules.

The subprime lending market had largely collapsed by the time the bill was introduced, so a law aimed at the origination practices of that market would have arrived after most of the harm it targeted had already occurred.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the consumers it covers, the protections are real and mostly low-cost to the public: honest disclosure, trained originators, and court access instead of forced arbitration address practices that cost borrowers their homes and their day in court. The genuine cost falls on lenders and arbitration-using businesses, and the main honest objection is that certification costs could restrict credit for marginal subprime borrowers. On balance the consumer benefits are larger, though the bill's scope (limited to subprime loans on the mortgage side) and its reliance on agency rulemaking would have muted its impact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcia Fudge introduced the bill on April 27, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
No other member cosponsored the bill, and the committee took no further action on it for the remainder of the 111th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without the bill ever receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subprime mortgage lenders and brokers never faced the certification, penalty, and fee-disclosure requirements, and businesses that use mandatory arbitration clauses kept the ability to route consumer disputes out of court. Borrowers and consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Marcia Fudge
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remaining twenty months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held on the bill; its only support was a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever tested.

industries.note: The bill would have required HUD certification and testing for anyone originating or brokering subprime loans, exposed them to daily civil penalties for unfair or deceptive practices, and barred undisclosed fees. Subprime lenders and brokers had earned fees and above-market rates from these borrowers, so the compliance burden and penalty exposure ran directly against the borrowers' interest in honest loans.

industries.industry: Businesses that use mandatory arbitration clauses (banks, card issuers, and other consumer firms)
industries.note: The bill would have made forced arbitration unenforceable across all consumer contracts, not just mortgages, restoring consumers' access to courts. These businesses benefit from arbitration because it shields them from consumer lawsuits, so their interest ran against the consumers the provision protects.

The bill would have authorized $2 million per year in grants to these nonprofits to educate borrowers about predatory lending practices — a small new funding stream that serves the same consumers the rest of the bill protects.
